lesson.title: Where Yes Turns Into No: The Boundary Line
lesson.summary: The boundary line is the edge between the points that satisfy a linear inequality and the points that do not, and whether you draw it solid or dashed tells you which side of that edge belongs to the solution.
lesson.body:
When you graphed systems of linear equations, the picture was clean: two lines crossed at exactly one point, and that point was the only pair of numbers that made both equations true at once. Inequalities change the question. Instead of asking where two expressions give the exact same value, an inequality like y < 2x + 1 asks where one side is smaller, or larger, than the other. Because there are infinitely many points where that comparison holds, the solution to a single linear inequality in two variables is not a point or even a line, it is an entire shaded region of the coordinate plane.

To find that region, you still need the line itself, and that line is called the boundary line. You get it by temporarily replacing the inequality symbol with an equals sign. For y < 2x + 1, the boundary line is y = 2x + 1, the same kind of line you already know how to graph from slope and y-intercept. The boundary line splits the entire plane into two halves: every point on one side makes the inequality true, and every point on the other side makes it false.

How you draw that line matters. If the inequality is strict, using < or >, the points exactly on the line are not part of the solution, because those points make the two sides equal rather than truly less than or greater than. You draw the boundary as a dashed line to show that this edge is not included. If the inequality allows equality, using ≤ or ≥, the points on the line do satisfy it, so you draw a solid line.

Here is a full example. Graph y < 2x + 1. Start with the boundary line y = 2x + 1: slope 2, y-intercept 1. Since the inequality is strict, draw it dashed. Now pick a test point that is clearly not on the line, the origin (0, 0) is usually easiest. Substitute it into the inequality: is 0 < 2(0) + 1? That simplifies to 0 < 1, which is true. Since the test point makes the inequality true, you shade the entire side of the boundary line that contains (0, 0), which is the region below the line. Every point in that shaded region, and no point above the dashed line, solves y < 2x + 1.

This is exactly the same skill you used for graphing systems, extended. When you graph two inequalities together, you draw two boundary lines and shade two regions. The overlap of those shaded regions, the part of the plane where both shadings occur, plays the same role that the single intersection point played for a system of equations: it is the set of every point that satisfies both conditions at once.
